The Hidden Life of Tidepools

By Marina Okafor

Twice a day the ocean pulls back and leaves behind small worlds in the rocks. A tidepool can swing from cold seawater to a warm, salty bath in a few hours, and the animals that live there have to survive both. Sea anemones close up to hold water, while hermit crabs trade shells as they grow.

Who lives there

  • Ochre sea stars, which can pull mussels open with steady pressure
  • Purple urchins that grind shallow pits into solid rock
  • Sculpins, small fish that blend into the algae

The pools are crowded because they are productive. Sunlight reaches the bottom, algae grow fast, and every crack offers shelter from waves and from the gulls that patrol the shore at low tide.

Tide heights at Point Sur

Time Height (ft)
05:12 -0.8
11:40 4.9

If you visit, step only on bare rock, put animals back exactly where you found them, and keep an eye on the incoming tide. A pool that was knee-deep at noon can be over your head an hour later.
